@@94531333 <h> Researchers are working to help make New England woodlands more resilient <p> The researcher team led a field tour in June attended by DEEP Commissioner Katie Dykes , Deputy Commissioner Mason Trumble , Director of the Office of Climate Planning Rebecca French , and State Forester Christopher Martin . Credit : University of Connecticut <p> The sounds of chainsaws and woodchippers and the sights of stands of dead trees have become more familiar in recent years across Connecticut . Forests are under stress and are being lost -- an average of 13 acres of forests lost per day since 1985 -- prompting an urgent question : what does the future of Connecticut 's forests look like ? <p> A team of UConn researchers including Department of Natural Resources and the Environment Associate Professor of Applied Forest Ecology and Director of the UConn Forest Robert Fahey , and Associate Extension Professor Tom Worthley are trying to help give our woodlands a fighting chance by developing strategies to build resilience in the face of the intersecting challenges trees face in our changing climate . <p> Forest management , or silviculture , is described as both an art and a science @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to achieve a desirable outcome . The outcomes could be sustainable timber production , habitat restoration for wildlife , or preserving forests for the innumerable benefits they provide for the whole ecosystem . <p> Worthley explains how a group of researchers published a paper to promote " Adaptive Silviculture for Climate Change " ( ASCC ) and develop a nationwide research network in which they proposed different silvicultural approaches to improve the health , diversity , and productivity of forests as the climate changes . <p> The resulting national ASCC project fosters collaboration between foresters , scientists , and other stakeholders , encouraging regional project teams to design treatments relevant to different regions and to develop site-specific solutions . <p> Fahey and Worthley are applying similar methods to New England forests with the Southern New England Exurban Affiliate Oak project , which is implemented on sites in Eastern Connecticut and Western Rhode Island . <p> Anticipated climatic changes are many , explains Worthley . These include meteorological shifts away from what trees have evolved to thrive in , including conditions such as wild temperature swings in the wintertime to periods @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ frequent and stronger storms . These variable conditions are pushing many species of tree to their limits . <p> Fahey adds that the arrival of invasive species like the emerald ash borer and the spongy moth add to the challenges trees face , in addition to development pressures that reduce overall forest cover and fragment the landscape . <p> " There are all these disturbance interactions layered upon each other and the trees are having to deal with it all at once , " Fahey says . " That leads to novel conditions and mortality events like the spongy moth outbreak , which was also layered on top of one of the most intense droughts in the last 100 years . We think that interaction is what led to the high levels of mortality . " <p> Climate adaptation experts have promoted the adoption of three potential silvicultural approaches to adapting forests to changing climate : resistance , resilience , and transition . <p> A resistance treatment aims to maintain the status quo in species mix and age structure , says Worthley , to essentially promote health and growth of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ largely dominated by oak and hickory canopies with subcanopies of more shade-tolerant hardwoods . This approach seeks to maintain this mix and is being tested along with the other strategies at the UConn and Mohegan State Forest research sites . <p> A resilience treatment attempts to create age class diversity within the stands , says Worthley . With this approach , managers try to achieve a mix of some old trees and some young trees and some in-between trees and to try to give some competitive advantage to new oak and hickory seedlings that will form future generations of our forests . <p> Transition treatments encourage a suite of species that are likely to have an advantage in future climates . Growing zones are and will continue to shift , changing the range of different species . Researchers note species that are native to Connecticut but tend to be found in the southern part of the state , then they see what they can do to encourage some of those species to grow in more northern locations . <p> For instance , where oaks and ashes have succumbed and site @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ poplar , a species that has traditionally been more frequently found in southern Connecticut but is now making its way further north . <p> " One of the interesting twists on our transition treatment sites is the reintroduction of hybrid American Chestnut because it 's a traditional species that was always here , " says Worthley . <p> " It 's a species that is not particularly tolerant of shade so is well suited to grow in the openings that have been created by the loss of oak trees from the spongy moth . " A hundred years ago , American chestnuts that had been dominant members of the forest canopy were being lost to the chestnut blight . <p> Connecticut 's landscape is unique , with non-contiguous , fragmented stretches of forest . The other national ASCC research areas are around 400-500 acres -- much larger than what could be tried in exurban Southern New England . As a result , the plots installed in Mohegan State Forest in the town of Scotland and the Lee Farm Tract in the UConn Forest mimic the parceled and fragmented forest conditions @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ says the overall development of management prescriptions uses an approach often called co-development , a process that brings together scientists , practitioners , and other stakeholders to create future-focused management plans together . <p> " This is partly a site-level and regionally focused project where treatments and implementation are meant as a demonstration that can then be used to do research , but also as a demonstration that can show some practices that can be used broadly across the region and adopted as we 're trying to promote climate adaptation in the region , " Fahey says . <p> The team is working with collaborators from the University of Rhode Island , where they have a parallel installation of treatments and have done a co-development process with slightly different treatments for the context of Rhode Island , which was hit even harder by the spongy moth , says Fahey . <p> " We 're also planning to implement another replicate of the project at the Lee Farm Tract of the UConn Forest , which we use for research and outreach around forest management and specifically , will be used as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ forests . " <p> This has meant engaging students with hands-on experiences , with undergraduates working as research technicians and on the UConn Forest Crew , which has been very rewarding for the team . Amanda Bunce , a Ph.D . student in Fahey 's lab , is researching social science aspects of engaging with stakeholders as they develop forest management prescriptions . <p> Fahey says there has been much interest in this work at the state level and beyond . The team led a field tour in June attended by DEEP Commissioner Katie Dykes , Deputy Commissioner Mason Trumble , Director of the Office of Climate Planning Rebecca French , and State Forester Christopher Martin . As part of the Governor 's Council on Climate Change and the Forest and Working Lands working group , Fahey sees growing support in trying to understand how to apply climate adaptation in our forests more broadly . <p> " This is a good starting point to bring to the state which must involve , not just state lands , but also private landowners , " he says . <p> " We 're @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ forests can promote climate adaptation and climate resiliency if it 's done right . We can use this to encourage active participation in understanding and using forests across the state rather than just turning them all into new housing developments . If people see the value of forests as a climate mitigation tool , we can actively promote climate adaptation and that 's to the benefit of maintaining forests for the future . " <p> Worthley notes that forests are seen as one of the solutions for climate change because trees sequester and store carbon ; but to do that , a forest needs to be healthy , productive , and resilient . <p> " The problem is that nature just is n't natural anymore because of the unanticipated consequences of the actions of human beings in the landscape , " Worthley says . <p> " We have air pollution , water pollution , deer over-abundance , absence of fire , non-native invasive plants and invasive insects and the solutions to these problems require intervention or management to keep the forest healthy and productive . These are the issues we @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to have strategies to offer various owners , whether it 's land trusts , the state , or private landowners . We hope to be able to offer ideas to help them manage the stresses that are anticipated with a changing climate , so they can continue to enjoy the benefits , rewards and satisfactions that come with being good land stewards . That 's what the experiments are all about . " <p> Citation : Researchers are working to help make New England woodlands more resilient ( 2022 , October 31 ) retrieved 31 October 2022 from https : **39;3976;TOOLONG ... @@94531335 <h> ' Earth is in our hands ' : Astronaut Pesquet 's plea for the planet <p> by Juliette Collen <p> While on the ISS , French astronaut Thomas Pesquet watched the " sinister spectacle " of hurricanes , tornadoes and fires storm across Earth . <p> From his unique viewpoint hundreds of kilometres above Earth , French astronaut Thomas Pesquet told AFP he felt helpless watching fires rage across the planet below , calling for more to be done to protect this fragile " island of life " . <p> Pesquet said his two tours onboard the International Space Station convinced him more than ever that the world is failing to address the threat posed by climate change . <p> He also witnessed moments of astonishing beauty while in space , some of which are captured in 300 photos published in his new book " La Terre entre nos mains " ( Earth is in our Hands ) , released this week in France , the profits of which will go to charity . <p> Pesquet wrote that he initially " caught the photo bug " during his first tour on the ISS in 2016-2017 . <p> But @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ November 2021 , that he fully embraced the endeavour , taking constant photos and sharing his passion with his colleagues in space . <p> " At first I was a bit of a Sunday photographer , then I really got a taste for it , " Pesquet told AFP in an interview . <p> " When you to arrive at the station , you have that smartphone reflex : you see something great and want to immortalise it , " he said . <p> " But quickly you are confronted with limitations , if you want to take photos at night , for example , or of precise targets with long lenses , " he added . <p> " It 's difficult because everything is manual " . <p> Pesquet , left , during a spacewalk outside the ISS in June , 2021 . <p> 245,000 photos <p> Around a dozen cameras are available to astronauts on the ISS , some permanently installed on the Cupula observation module , some in the US laboratory which has a porthole looking down on Earth . <p> Despite only having a few hours @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ during his last tour . <p> " Many are not very good , but in six months there is a real progression curve , " he said . <p> Throughout the photos of rivers , oceans , deserts , mountains , sunsets and sunrises , the astronaut 's amazement at the world shines through . <p> " The planet is so vast and diverse that you still do n't feel like you 've seen everything . Even after 400 days in orbit , there are still some thing that surprise me , places I have n't seen , " he said . <p> The speed of the station , which hurtles through space at 28,000 kilometres an hour , means that " we are never above the same area at the same time of day , " he said . <p> One day , he was surprised to find out that the northern lights appeared blue from space . <p> Pesquet only managed to get a photo of the phenomenon because his US colleague Shane Kimbrough told him it was taking place , after spotting it out of his bedroom @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tour onboard the ISS . <p> ' Sinister spectacle ' <p> But Pesquet did not only witness Earth 's beauty . <p> He also captured images of a world in a state of degradation : the " sinister spectacle " of hurricanes , tornadoes and fires that stormed across the planet during his second stint of 200 days in space . <p> Pesquet described himself as a " helpless " witness to the carnage . <p> " What struck me the most were the fires . " he trailed off . <p> " Every year we say ' now is the time act ' -- and it 's the same the next year , we only make small changes without a strong global impact . @@94531923 <p> In 2019 , three dozen leading researchers sounded a stark warning in a prominent scientific journal : To fight climate change and improve human health , the world needed to dramatically cut back on eating red meat . <p> The findings were quickly attacked by Frank Mitloehner , the head of an agricultural research center at the University of California , Davis , and a prominent critic of the journal 's research . <p> The report 's authors were spreading a " radical anti-meat agenda , " Mitloehner wrote on Twitter , where he led a backlash under the hashtag , #yes2meat . " Their so-called planetary diet is a quasi-vegan diet , " he said , calling the findings " anti-livestock . " <p> According to internal University of California documents reviewed by The New York Times , Mitloehner 's academic group , the CLEAR Center at UC Davis , receives almost all its funding from industry donations and coordinates with a major livestock lobby group on messaging campaigns . <p> The documents show that the center , which has become a leading institution in the field of agriculture and climate , was set up in 2019 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ several years from the Institute for Feed Education and Research , or IFeeder , the nonprofit arm of the American Feed Industry Association , a livestock industry group that represents major agricultural companies like Cargill and Tyson . <p> As of April 2022 , the CLEAR Center had also received more than $350,000 from other industry or corporate sources , the documents show , including nearly $200,000 from the California Cattle Council , a regional livestock industry group . <p> The documents were obtained by Unearthed , the investigative arm of Greenpeace U.K. , under freedom of information laws . The New York Times also independently obtained the files from officials at UC Davis . <p> The CLEAR Center has acknowledged receiving philanthropic gifts , including from IFeeder , but the extent of the private funding and collaboration were not previously known . <p> There is no indication that Mitloehner or the CLEAR Center violated disclosure requirements . California requires researchers to disclose funding from private donors but exempts funding received from nonprofit groups . Because IFeeder , formally known as the Institute for Feed Education &amp; Research , is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ not subject to detailed state disclosure rules . <p> The CLEAR Center said in a statement that it discloses funding in line with University of California policy . The university deferred questions to the CLEAR Center . <p> In written responses to detailed questions , Mitloehner said the livestock industry 's financial and other ties to his research center were instrumental to the center 's mission . " I can not help the livestock sector reduce its environmental impact without working directly with its members , " he said . <p> He also highlighted the work that his lab was doing with the industry to reduce its emissions of greenhouse gases , including investigating feed additives that could help reduce belching by cattle , a major source of planet-warming methane . <p> Critics say that close financial ties between a research center and the industry it studies create the potential for conflict of interest . <p> " Industry funding does not necessarily compromise research , but it does inevitably have a slant on the directions with which you ask questions and the tendency to interpret those results in a way @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ an assistant professor in environmental studies at New York University . <p> " Almost everything that I 've seen from Dr. Mitloehner 's communications has downplayed every impact of livestock , " he said . " <p> Lara Moody , executive director of IFeeder , said the group funded the CLEAR Center to further scientific research and discourse on animal agriculture 's environmental effects . <p> " We believe it is critical that there is a two-way dialogue between public and private entities involved in the manufacture of America 's food supply if we are to make progress on achieving overarching food security and climate goals , " she said in a statement . <p> Ranching is a significant contributor to global warming . @@94532021 <p> Religion and science have never been fast friends , but they 'd better become better friends fast . <p> The global ecological crisis is an existential threat that calls for all sectors of society to work together to preserve our human habitat . While this includes responsible participation from the business community and government , religious leaders and scientists must overcome their historic antipathy that thwarts planet-saving action . <p> Science has reason for its frustration with religion . From Galileo 's house arrest for holding that the Earth revolves around the Sun , to John Scopes ' conviction for teaching human evolution , to skepticism over COVID-19 vaccinations , religion has failed to show itself a trustworthy partner in the general pursuit of truth . On the other hand , religion has had legitimate qualms with science 's failure to acknowledge its own limits . Misguided theories of eugenics , the development of the atomic bomb , and unchecked advances in artificial intelligence threaten human dignity and life itself . In each case , religion could contribute moral guidance to scientific pursuits , which by their nature do not otherwise address these matters . <p> It 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ticking , and we are running out of time to reverse the devastating effects of human behavior on the planet . While we must urge the fossil fuel industry to transition quicker to cleaner energy and press politicians to support the same , conjuring support for solutions from religion and science will be crucial . <p> Just getting religion to defer to science , however , will not be enough , as science sometimes overestimates its capacity to solve problems through technological means alone . The faith community will need to do its part to nurture moral agency and urgency for changes in personal , corporate and public behavior . <p> Every religion must draw upon its own spiritual teachings to contribute to this effort to bend the curve of opinion toward ecological conservation . Tuesday night at SMU , faith leaders from the Buddhist , Jewish , Christian and Muslim traditions will be doing just that in a symposium titled Confronting Our Global Ecological Crisis , sponsored by the Museum of World Religions ( Prothro Great Hall , 7 p.m. , free to the public ) . <p> Speaking @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ only if we begin to read Scripture more critically . We can not continue to allow selective passages that speak of the Earth 's destruction in the end time to guide our concern ( or lack of it ) for creation care . Even if one holds to this view -- which need not be the case , as apocalyptic language should be interpreted figuratively rather than literally -- Christians should not only love our neighbor as ourselves in the time remaining , but also love the world our neighbor inhabits with us , if only for today . <p> When the reformer Martin Luther was asked what he would do if the world were to end tomorrow , he said : " I would plant an apple tree today . " We can and must act likewise in our time to do all we can to heal the ills of our planet and promote its good health as a priority that supersedes short-term thinking about economic prosperity at all costs . The cost is too great to continue down this path . <p> Climate change is wreaking economic havoc @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ dollars of unbudgeted relief money annually that add to federal deficits and the national debt . Supply chain interruptions slow commerce and add to inflation . A heating planet is destroying crops and driving migration , impacting jobs , wages and markets . Stemming global warming is paramount to stabilizing human life and culture . <p> The early church theologian , Irenaeus of Lyon , said that God created the world with two hands : word and wisdom . Traditionally , religion has focused on knowledge that comes by revelation through the word of God that is to be heard and obeyed . But wisdom is also a source of knowledge from God , only it comes about by observation of the world God has made . The latter approach is amenable to the scientific process of discovery . It is not contrary to religious knowing ; it is complementary to it , if not a form of it . <p> " The earth is the Lord 's and all that is in it , the world , and those who live in it , " the psalmist said . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ any more than Earth is opposed to the heavens . Both are God 's creation , and in the end , the Bible also says we are to look for a new creation -- new in kind , that is , not new in number . This promised renewal envisions nonhuman creation experiencing its own redemption and fulfillment of divine purpose . <p> We honor God best when we care well for creation . We ca n't do it alone . We need all the partners we can get , whether they share our faith or not . The time is now to overcome the enmity between religion and science in the common interest of healing and preserving our planet . <p> The Rev. George A. Mason is founder and president of Faith Commons , adjunct professor at Perkins School of Theology and senior pastor emeritus of Wilshire Baptist Church . He wrote this column for The Dallas Morning News .

@@94532830 <h> NC State gets $6.5 million to innovate fertilizer production and address global climate change <p> NC State is aiming to innovate the energy-intensive production of fertilizer to make the process more sustainable and help reduce carbon dioxide emissions . <p> Posted 8:53 p.m . Today -- Updated 9:08 p.m . Today <p> By Liz McLaughlin , WRAL Climate Change Reporter <p> NC State announced a research collaboration to uncover biology-based ways to address global climate change . <p> The project aims to reduce carbon emissions and develop environmentally-friendly paths to fertilizer production . Currently , the process of creating the fertilizer required to feed the world 's growing population is a very energy-intensive process . One of the key components in fertilizer , ammonia , requires temperatures of around 930 degrees Fahrenheit to manufacture . That process contributes to up to 2% of the world 's carbon dioxide emissions , according to the Institute for Industrial Productivity . <p> The project , called the Biocatalyst Interactions with Gases , or BIG , Collaboration , is funded by the Novo Nordisk Foundation . The researchers will receive 6.5 million dollars in funding across 5 years . NC State will @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> " It 's big , because we we need to have a lot of different disciplines , a lot of different competencies represented on the team , because the problems are really complex and it is really about collaborating together to tackle these huge challenges , " said Sonja Salmon , a lead researcher on the project with a background in textiles and enzymology . <p> NC State 's textile school is aiming to find a new approach to making production cleaner by designing enzyme-soaked filters to capture nitrogen . <p> " Through discussing with my collaborators , we landed on nitrogen as being a critical gas to combat , maybe equally critical to carbon dioxide in some ways between carbon dioxide and converting nitrogen to ammonia , " Salmon said . " These are incredibly important , basic fundamental reactions in nature that can help us move to a more resilient bioeconomy , which is what we need to be able to mitigate climate change and be able to feed the world . " <p> The project will aim to utilize the nitrogenase enzyme that 's abundant in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ able to convert nitrogen to ammonia at room temperature , which could revolutionize the manufacturing process and significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions , if the team is able to innovate the biochemistry process and replicate it on a large scale .
